extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students working through textbook exercises (proofs/real analysis/introductory abstract math)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and heuristics for constructing and writing proofs for undergraduate-level math exercises (set theory, sequences, suprema, relations, congruence, functions, injections/surjections, cardinality, contradictions). Emphasises common proof techniques and pitfalls with worked examples and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove two sets equal by mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A = B, show each set is a subset of the other: A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the approach 'take an arbitrary element of one set and show it belongs to the other'. The text exemplifies this for intervals and other sets; sometimes one direction is straightforward while the other requires a construction (e.g. choosing N large enough).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show membership in intersections of shrinking intervals using an N
rubrics_metrics.description: Given y ∈ (0,1), produce N ∈ N so that 1/N ≤ y ≤ 1 − 1/N (or analogous inequalities) to show membership in an intersection ⋂_{n=3}^∞ (1/n, 1−1/n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the inequalities for N (e.g. N ≥ 1/y and N ≥ 1/(1−y)) and take N = max(⌈1/y⌉, ⌈1/(1−y)⌉) (or +1 as scratchwork suggests). Write the choices and justify they satisfy the bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive to prove membership of intersections equal closed interval
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ⋂_{n=1}^∞ (−1/n,1+1/n) ⊆ [0,1], prove the contrapositive: if y ∉ [0,1], then y ∉ ⋂_{n=1}^∞ (−1/n,1+1/n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split into cases y<0 and y>1; for y<0 pick N with y < −1/N; for y>1 pick N with 1+1/N < y (e.g. N > 1/(y−1)). Use these Ns to show y fails to lie in a particular interval, so not in the intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize maximum and supremum via upper bounds and leastness
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a is max(S) or sup(S): (1) show a is an upper bound for S, and (2) show any number less than a fails to be an upper bound (i.e. a is the least upper bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For maximum, additionally show a ∈ S. For examples: [1,3] has max=3 because 3∈[1,3] and any number <3 is not an upper bound; (1,3) has no max but sup=3 by same least-upper-bound argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: When working with integer-valued sets, simplify by reversing equivalent algebraic steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate inequalities algebraically (divide, add) and reason that steps are reversible to identify the integer set; then deduce maximum/supremum from integer bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: solve |2(m−4)| ≤ 15 by dividing and adding then interpreting the resulting real interval intersection with Z to get integer endpoints and hence maximum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a set has no maximum by constructing a larger element
rubrics_metrics.description: To show S has no maximum, prove for any x∈S there exists another element of S greater than x (so x is not an upper bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: S = {2 − 1/n : n∈N}. Given x = 2 − 1/n, choose m>n to get 2 − 1/m > x. For suprema, show 2 is an upper bound and that any a<2 fails to be an upper bound by picking n with 1/n < 2−a (n = ⌈1/(2−a)⌉ + 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding boundedness and lack of supremum via unbounded sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subset contains arbitrarily large elements (e.g. {πk : k∈Z}), then it has no upper bound and hence no maximum or supremum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate explicit unbounded growth—here πk → +∞ as k→+∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute max of union S ∪ T by taking max{s,t}
rubrics_metrics.description: If s = max S and t = max T (or suprema), then max(S∪T) = max{s,t}; prove by showing max{s,t} is an upper bound for S∪T and least among such bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two properties: (i) it bounds every element of S∪T, (ii) any upper bound b of S∪T satisfies max{s,t} ≤ b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze suprema of intersections with edge cases (empty intersection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When investigating sup(S∩T), consider various configurations: one containing the other, overlapping, or disjoint. If S∩T = ∅, then every real number is an upper bound, so no least upper bound exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit examples to guide conjecture; treat empty intersection as a special case with no supremum in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove sup(S+T) = s+t using contrapositive and epsilon splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a = s + t is the least upper bound of S+T, show a is an upper bound and if b < a then b is not an upper bound by writing b = u+v with u<s and v<t and producing c∈S,d∈T with c>u,d>v so c+d>b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit choice: set u = s − ε, v = t − ε with ε = (a − b)/2; then find c>d as above to contradict b being an upper bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monotonicity and least-upper-bound property to show convergence to supremum
rubrics_metrics.description: For an increasing sequence (a_n) with supremum a, given ε>0 pick N with a_N > a − ε (because a−ε is not an upper bound), then for all n ≥ N, a_n ≥ a_N > a − ε, and trivial upper tail bound gives |a_n − a| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unwrap |a_n − a| < ε into a − ε < a_n < a + ε and argue the right inequality holds automatically if a is an upper bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check relation properties systematically and supply explicit counterexamples when failing
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity, inspect definitions; if a property may fail, provide explicit counterexample functions/values rather than mere claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g. a relation 'f ℛ g if they are equal at some point' is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive—need to produce f,g,h and points x≠y to witness failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove congruence relation sparsity implies n=1 via divisibility reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If the congruence modulo n relation is not sparse (some a≡b and also a≡b+1), deduce n divides both (b−a) and (b+1−a) hence divides their difference 1, forcing n=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply divisibility and properties of natural numbers (n∈N) to conclude impossibility except n=1; check the converse that n=1 gives the full relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of multiplicative inverse modulo p: use Bézout's identity
rubrics_metrics.description: To find k with n k ≡ 1 (mod p), it suffices that gcd(n,p)=1; Bézout guarantees integers x,y with xn+yp=1 so xn≡1 (mod p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show gcd(n,p)=1 is necessary (if p does not divide n) and sufficient via Bézout; give counterexamples for composite modulus when gcd>1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Bézout's identity to relate gcd and divisibility conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bézout: there exist x,y with gcd(a,d)=xa+yd; can be manipulated (divide by gcd) to deduce divisibility consequences like (d/gcd(a,d)) | b when d | ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite equations dividing both a and d by gcd and multiply as needed; show how to extract divisibility relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine integrality conditions for Diophantine functional definitions via divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function definition requires integer outputs (e.g. y = (6 − a x)/b with y∈Z for all x∈Z), derive necessary divisibility constraints (e.g. b | 6 and b | a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plug particular x values (x=0) to derive immediate constraints; characterize all solutions by letting 6 = k b and a = ℓ b then showing y = k − ℓ x ∈ Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove image/range containment by bounding and solving algebraically
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f(R) ⊆ [−1,1] for f(x)=2x/(1+x^2), manipulate inequality −1 ≤ 2x/(1+x^2) ≤ 1 using known non-negativity (1+x^2 ≥ 1) and algebra to reduce to squares, then reverse reasoning to write a direct proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For surjectivity onto [−1,1], solve quadratic y = 2x/(1+x^2) for x: rearrange to quadratic in x, handle special case y=0 separately, and ensure one solution is real for each y∈[−1,1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze quadratics via completing the square for injectivity/surjectivity facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the square for f(x)=x^2+ax+b to find its minimum (vertex) and argue about surjectivity (range) and injectivity (two-to-one except on monotone half-rays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the vertex and shape (parabola up/down) to deduce not injective on whole R and not surjective to R when bounded below/above; restrict domains if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduce injective self-maps on N with f(n) ≤ n are identity via (strong) induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f:N→N injective and f(n) ≤ n for all n, prove f(n) = n for all n by induction: base cases force f(1)=1 etc., and injectivity prevents collisions, leading to f(n)=n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply strong induction: knowing f(k)=k for k<n helps show f(n) cannot be any smaller value already used, hence equals n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a function on equivalence classes is well-defined by checking independence of representative
rubrics_metrics.description: If f maps equivalence classes [(x,y)] to some value depending only on the class (e.g. radius r = √(x^2+y^2)), show that if [(x,y)]=[(s,t)] then outputs agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove: equality of classes implies same defining invariant (here same radius), so mapping does not depend on representative. Then show injectivity/surjectivity by constructing preimages for each value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define canonical remainder representative map Zn → {0,...,n−1} and prove bijectivity via Euclidean division
rubrics_metrics.description: Given [z]_n ∈ Z_n map to the remainder r from Euclidean division z = qn + r with 0≤r≤n−1; show well-definedness (same remainder for congruent classes), injectivity (same remainder ⇒ congruent), and surjectivity (every remainder attained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniqueness and bounds on remainders and standard Euclidean algorithm facts as the proof backbone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove/disprove algebraic function identities by pointwise evaluation and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To test identities like f◦(g+h) = f◦g + f◦h, evaluate both sides at arbitrary x and compare; if equality would require special structure (e.g. f linear), produce a counterexample (e.g. f(x)=x^2) to disprove in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For positive identities, give algebraic derivation pointwise; for negatives, give explicit non-linear f or particular values to show failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle function-division/composition subtleties carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Identities like (1/f)◦g = 1/(f◦g) hold by definition; but f◦(1/g) = ? requires f(1/x) = 1/f(x), which is not generally true, so the identity fails in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit counterexample: f(x)=x+2 demonstrates 1/f(x) ≠ f(1/x). Always check the needed functional equation before asserting such equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct counterexamples to set-image equalities by designing collisions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f(W∩X) may not equal f(W)∩f(X), pick W and X with small intersection but design f mapping distinct elements to the same value so f(W) and f(X) overlap more than f(W∩X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard image/preimage inclusions and exhibit strictness with non-surjective functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Always remember f(f^{-1}(Y)) ⊆ Y; strict inclusion occurs when f is not surjective and Y contains elements outside the range. Provide a concrete example to show Y ⊄ f(f^{-1}(Y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f:{1,2}→{1,2,3} with f identity and Y={2,3}; 3∈Y but 3∉f(f^{-1}(Y)) since 3 has no preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find inverses by solving the equation y = f(x) for x and checking domain constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f is bijective and compute f^{-1}, solve y = f(x) algebraically for x, ensure solution is in domain and well-defined; you may instead propose g and verify left and right inverse properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for rational-form functions, isolate x (algebraic manipulations) and note forbidden values like y=1 in x = (1−2y)/(y−1) etc.; verify g◦f = id and f◦g = id to conclude bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove non-existence statements via modular arithmetic contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove no integer solutions exist for Diophantine equations, reduce modulo small integers to derive impossible congruences (e.g. square residues modulo 4 or 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 5y^2 − 4x^2 = 7 reduces mod 4 to y^2 ≡ 3 (mod 4) impossible; or mod 5 eliminates x using quadratic residues table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction/minimal counterexample for 'no smallest positive rational' type statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume existence of smallest positive rational r, then show r/2 is positive rational and < r, contradiction. For irrationals, assume r minimal and show r/2 irrational via contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern for nonexistence/minimality arguments: produce a strictly smaller candidate of the same kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality proofs via algebraic rearrangement into squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Many inequalities can be proved by rearranging to an obvious nonnegative square term, e.g. (x−y)^2 > 0 to show x/y + y/x > 2 when x≠y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work backwards in scratchwork from the known nonnegative expression to the desired inequality when writing the final direct proof; multiply by positive denominators carefully to preserve inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show strict inequality equalities impossible by clearing denominators and obtaining positive-square contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show 2/a + 2/b ≠ 4/(a+b) for positive a,b, clear denominators to get a^2 + b^2 = 0, impossible for positive a,b—hence contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method converts a proposed equality into an impossible algebraic statement under given positivity constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish denumerability by explicit bijections or diagonalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a set is denumerable, either construct an explicit bijection to N or use diagonalization/known results about products of denumerable sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: N×N is denumerable via diagonal argument; shifting/scaling Q by π gives bijections to Q and preserves denumerability; use log to give bijection (0,∞)↔R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct bijections between intervals and R via elementary functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Map (0,∞)↔R by log, (−∞,−29)↔R by composition with sign/shift e.g. h(x)=log(−x−29). Piecewise rational functions can also be built to map (0,1)↔R by blowing up at endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building piecewise maps, ensure continuity/surjectivity properties as needed or prove bijectivity by showing explicit inverses.
